# Hours, Output and the Pilot Problem: A Re-examination of the Halden Reduced-Hours Pilot

*Comment, Journal of Labour and Organisation Studies. K. Varga and T. Holm, Centre for Applied Labour Statistics.*

## Abstract

The Halden pilot reported that 61 organisations maintained output while cutting scheduled hours by 20%, implying a 23.4% gain in output per hour. Using the pilot's microdata, released under the Institute's data-sharing policy, we re-examine the result. Four problems, each documented below, account for most of the reported gain: attrition that was not random, a manager-reported output measure that overstates output relative to organisations' own records, an hours denominator that counts scheduled rather than actual time, and an unadjusted revenue comparison. Correcting the first three, the gain in output per hour falls from 23.4% to 10.8% in the subset of organisations where correction is possible. We then argue that the remaining gain is plausibly a novelty effect, and that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty.

## 1. Attrition

The working paper states that nine of the 70 enrolled organisations "withdrew during the preparation phase, chiefly for scheduling reasons". The microdata tell a different story. Seven of the nine withdrew after the reduced schedule had begun: four in the first month and three in the second. In exit forms, six of the nine gave workload or inability to maintain output as the main reason, and two gave scheduling. The organisations that found the change hardest were therefore removed from the sample before the outcome was measured. With nine of 70 organisations missing, and those nine plausibly the least successful, the reported sample of 61 is a sample of survivors.

## 2. The output measure

The primary outcome was an index completed by a manager who was also the pilot's internal sponsor. Managers were asked to base the index on organisational records, but were not required to submit them. Twenty-three organisations did submit underlying records (billable hours delivered, tickets closed, units produced, or cases completed). For these 23 we can compare the manager's index with the index implied by the records.

**Table 1. Manager-reported and record-based output, 23 organisations with records**

| Measure | Mean output index (baseline = 100) |
|---|---|
| Manager-reported index | 98.9 |
| Index computed from submitted records | 95.1 |
| Difference | −3.8 points |

In 19 of the 23 organisations the manager-reported index exceeded the record-based index. We do not suggest bad faith. A manager responsible for a change he or she advocated, asked to rate its effect on a scale where 100 means "unchanged", will tend to round toward success. But the difference is systematic, and the headline output figure of 98.7 should not be taken at face value.

## 3. The hours denominator

The pilot computed output per hour by dividing output by the ratio of scheduled hours, 0.8. Twenty-seven organisations used time-tracking software throughout. Their data show average actual weekly hours of 40.3 at baseline and 34.6 during the pilot, a fall of 14.1% rather than 20%. The difference comes from two sources visible in the logs: longer working days on the remaining four days (average +0.7 hours per day), and work logged on the scheduled day off (on average 1.6 hours per week). Some further work on the day off is probably not logged.

Seventeen organisations have both submitted output records and time tracking. In this subset, record-based output was 95.4 and actual hours fell from 40.4 to 34.8 (−13.9%). The implied gain in output per actual hour is 10.8% (95.4 / 86.1), less than half the reported 23.4%.

**Table 2. Implied gain in output per hour under successive corrections**

| Specification | Output | Hours ratio | Gain per hour |
|---|---|---|---|
| As reported (all 61) | 98.7 | 0.800 | +23.4% |
| Record-based output, scheduled hours (23) | 95.1 | 0.800 | +18.9% |
| Manager-reported output, actual hours (27) | 98.4 | 0.859 | +14.6% |
| Record-based output, actual hours (17) | 95.4 | 0.861 | +10.8% |

## 4. Revenue

The working paper reports revenue 1.4% higher than in the previous year. This is a nominal comparison. Consumer prices rose by 4.1% over the same twelve months; in real terms, revenue in participating organisations fell by approximately 2.6%. Revenue is in any case a poor proxy for productivity, but the figure as presented gives a misleading impression of growth.

## 5. Sectoral claims

The pilot concluded that gains in output per hour were "found in every sector" and that the model is "sector-general". This conclusion is an artifact of the per-hour metric. When hours are cut by 20%, any output index above 80 will register as a per-hour gain. Retail and hospitality output fell by 6.9% on the manager-reported measure; the three retail and hospitality organisations among the 23 with records show a fall of 11.2%. A fall in output of this size in a customer-facing business is not evidence that reduced hours work there. The Varden County trial's counter and contact-centre stratum, the only randomised evidence on coverage-bound work, found a fall in output per employee of 11.4% and longer waits for the public. That is, in our view, the most reliable finding in the literature to date.

## 6. Novelty

After the corrections above, a gain in output per actual hour of about 11% remains in the subset of survivors with usable data. We think this residual should not be read as a durable effect. The pilot's own survey shows self-reported energy at work rising by 0.61 standard deviations at month three and falling to 0.29 at month six. Extrapolating this decline, energy would return to baseline at around month ten. A change that staff chose, welcomed and knew to be under evaluation is the classic setting for a novelty effect: effort rises while the change is new and observed, and falls back once it is routine. Six months is not long enough to distinguish a novelty effect from a durable one, and the burden of proof lies with those claiming the latter.

## 7. The meetings hypothesis

The Varden trial's authors report, in an unregistered exploratory analysis, that cuts in recurring meetings correlated with per-hour gains across seven treated offices, and suggest this as a mechanism. We regard this as a post hoc account fitted to a subgroup. A correlation across seven offices, selected for analysis after the results were known, is precisely the kind of finding that does not replicate. The meetings explanation has an intuitive appeal that has outrun its evidence, and it should not be cited as a mechanism.

## 8. Conclusion

Taking the problems together: attrition removed the organisations least able to cope; the output measure overstated output by roughly four points; the hours measure overstated the reduction in time by roughly six points; and the remaining gain coincides with a decaying measure of enthusiasm. We conclude that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the best-supported finding is the negative one: where output depends on presence, reduced hours reduce output.

We recommend that future evaluations use record-based output, actual hours, a randomised or at least matched comparison group, follow-up of at least eighteen months, and analysis of all enrolled organisations including those that withdraw.

## Data note

All re-analyses use the Halden pilot microdata (release 1.2). The corrections in Table 2 can only be computed for subsets of organisations, and those subsets were not chosen at random; organisations with time tracking and records may differ from the others. Our corrected estimates therefore describe those subsets, not the pilot as a whole.

# Review: Varga & Holm, "Hours, Output and the Pilot Problem" (Comment)

**Sections 1–4 are a valuable correction of the Halden pilot. The conclusion goes well beyond the evidence.** Using the microdata, the authors establish three things:

- The attrition was not what the working paper described.
- Managers' ratings ran above the organisations' own records.
- Actual hours fell by about 14%, not 20%.

These findings support "the reported gain is roughly halved." They don't support "entirely an artifact." The comment's own corrected estimate is still +10.8%. The novelty argument meant to remove that residual is untested. The randomised Varden trial, which the comment cites selectively, found a gain of similar size.

## Arithmetic check

| Item | Calculation | Result | Paper |
|---|---|---|---|
| Record-based, scheduled hours | 95.1 / 0.8 | 1.189 | +18.9% ✓ |
| Manager-reported, actual hours | 98.4 / 0.859 | 1.146 | +14.6% ✓ |
| Record-based, actual hours | 95.4 / 0.861 | 1.108 | +10.8% ✓ |
| Hours (27 organisations) | 34.6 / 40.3 | 0.859 | −14.1% ✓ |
| Hours (17 organisations) | 34.8 / 40.4 | 0.861 | −13.9% ✓ |
| Real revenue | 1.014 / 1.041 | 0.974 | −2.6% ✓ |
| Energy returns to baseline | 0.29 ÷ (0.32 / 3 months) ≈ 2.7 months after month 6 | ≈ month 9 | "around month ten" ✗ |

There are two numerical inconsistencies:

1. **The hours decomposition doesn't add up.** Four days at about 8.06 h (baseline 40.3 ÷ 5), plus 0.7 h a day, plus 1.6 h on the day off, gives about 36.6 h a week, not the reported 34.6 h. Even taking +0.7 against an 8 h scheduled day gives 36.4 h. The +0.7 and 1.6 figures are inconsistent with the total, or are measured against a different base. Please reconcile them.
2. **The energy extrapolation is slightly off.** A linear extrapolation reaches zero at about month nine, not month ten. This matters less than the fact that a straight line drawn through two points is weak evidence for anything (see section 6 below).

## Major issues

### 1. "Entirely an artifact" contradicts the comment's own results

- After the corrections, a positive gain of +10.8% remains.
- The only argument for setting that to zero is the novelty hypothesis, which the authors infer from a self-reported energy measure rather than from output (section 6 below).
- "In our assessment" doesn't rescue the claim. The abstract and conclusion state it as a finding.

The defensible conclusion is narrower: the corrected gain is roughly half the reported one, it applies to a non-random subset of survivors, and its durability is unknown.

### 2. Attrition is described as corrected, but it isn't

The abstract says "Correcting the first three" problems, and attrition is the first. Table 2 does not correct for attrition. All four rows use survivors only, as section 6 concedes ("the subset of survivors").

To actually correct for attrition, the authors could:

- report what output data exist for the nine organisations that withdrew, or
- produce a bounding analysis, for example assuming withdrawers had zero per-hour gain or the retail-level output fall.

As it stands, the attrition finding is a strong qualitative point but contributes nothing to the 10.8% figure.

A smaller point: the Halden pilot had a two-month preparation phase. "Four in the first month and three in the second" needs to say clearly that these are months of the reduced schedule, not of preparation. That distinction is the whole basis for the claim that the working paper was wrong.

### 3. Revenue is listed as accounting for the gain, but it can't

The abstract lists four problems that "account for most of the reported gain," including the revenue comparison. Revenue doesn't enter the output-per-hour calculation at all. The real-terms correction is right, but it belongs to a separate point about how the pilot was presented.

Deflating by CPI rather than by sector price indices is also rough. That is acceptable for a comment, but say so.

### 4. Varden is cited selectively

The comment calls Varden's counter-stratum finding "the most reliable finding in the literature to date." The same trial's case-processing stratum shows:

- randomised assignment, which addresses selection;
- record-based output, which addresses the measurement problem;
- timesheet actual hours, which addresses the hours denominator;
- a nine-month follow-up, longer than Halden's six months;
- and still a +12.5% gain in output per actual hour (CI +6.9 to +18.4).

That is close to the comment's own +10.8%. Taken together, the two studies look like **convergent evidence for a real gain of about 10–12% per actual hour in work not tied to presence.** That gain is smaller than first claimed and of uncertain durability, but it is not zero.

Varden's counter stratum also showed +6.7% per actual hour. The comment cites only the per-employee fall.

**A comment that builds its case on Varden's methods has to address the stratum where those methods found a gain.** Section 6 should also note that Varden's controls knew a trial was under way, which partly addresses the "observed" side of the novelty argument.

### 5. The record-based measure has its own problems

- **Some record-based measures are really input measures.** "Billable hours delivered" is one of the listed record types, and it falls almost mechanically when hours are cut. Any professional-services firms using it would show artificially low record-based output. Dividing by actual hours then measures utilisation, not productivity. Report the sector and record type for the 23 organisations, and rerun Table 2 excluding hours-based measures.
- **The weighting is unstated.** Halden used employee weights; the comment doesn't say which weights it used.
- **There are no confidence intervals.** None of the corrected estimates in Table 2 has one. With 17 to 27 organisations, the uncertainty is substantial.
- **The 19-of-23 result is well supported.** It is statistically clear (sign test p ≈ 0.001), and it is the comment's strongest finding.

### 6. The novelty argument doesn't test what it claims

- **It uses a proxy instead of output.** Halden's output index is *monthly*, and the authors have the microdata. If novelty drives the gain, output per hour should decline across months. Test that directly.
- **Energy is not productivity.** The conclusion also calls it "enthusiasm," which is a third concept.
- **Two points don't make a trend.** Linear extrapolation from two survey waves cannot identify a trend, let alone show where it ends.
- **"The burden of proof" is rhetoric.** Novelty is a hypothesis the comment proposes. It is fair to say six months cannot separate novelty from a lasting effect. Concluding that the effect *is* novelty requires evidence.

### 7. The meetings section misdescribes Varden

- **Varden's offices were not "selected for analysis after the results were known."** The seven offices were simply the treated case-processing stratum. The calendar data were collected in month six, before the nine-month results.
- **Varden made no strong mechanism claim.** It labelled the analysis exploratory, stressed that seven offices "cannot establish a mechanism," and registered a confirmatory test. The comment's position ("should not be cited as a mechanism") is essentially Varden's own caveat, presented as a rebuttal.
- **The real weakness goes unmentioned.** Varden has no baseline meeting data, so "offices that cut meetings most" can't actually be measured. That would be a stronger point than the one made.

## What the comment gets right and should lead with

- **Attrition happened after treatment began, and for reasons related to the outcome.** This is a clear misreport in the working paper and the comment's most important contribution.
- **Manager ratings exceed the records, systematically** (19 of 23).
- **Actual hours fell by about 14%, not 20%.** This replicates Varden's finding of 13% in case-processing.
- **The sector-general claim is a per-hour artifact,** and the retail and hospitality output falls are real.
- **Per-employee output fell by about 4.6% on records.** The comment underuses this. For an employer paying full wages, falling per-employee output is arguably the key practical figure, and it is better supported than the per-hour framing.
- **The recommendations are sound:** record-based output, actual hours, comparison groups, long follow-up, and intention-to-treat analysis.

## Suggested revisions

1. Replace "entirely an artifact" with a bounded conclusion: roughly half the reported gain, in a non-random subset of survivors, with durability unknown.
2. Either correct for attrition with a bounding analysis, or remove it from "correcting the first three."
3. Remove revenue from the list of problems that "account for" the per-hour gain.
4. Engage with Varden's case-processing result.
5. Test novelty directly using the monthly output index.
6. Check the hours decomposition and the month-ten extrapolation.
7. Add confidence intervals to Table 2, and check the record types used for record-based output.
8. Correct the description of Varden's meetings analysis, and replace it with the baseline-data critique.

I can draft a revised abstract and conclusion in the bounded form if that would help.
